claim: ATP7A null mutations cause neurodegeneration.
source: We focused on copper and its transporter ATP7A because ATP7A null mutations cause neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about ATP7A.

claim: ATP7A immunoaffinity chromatography identified 541 proteins co-isolating with ATP7A.
source: We performed ATP7A immunoaffinity chromatography and identified 541 proteins co-isolating with ATP7A.
evidence: This is a direct experimental result reported in the abstract and supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: The ATP7A interactome concentrated gene products implicated in neurodegeneration and neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: The ATP7A interactome concentrated gene products implicated in neurodegeneration and neurodevelopmental disorders, including subunits of the Golgi-localized conserved oligomeric Golgi (COG) complex.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis of the interactome shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: COG null cells possess altered content and subcellular localization of ATP7A.
source: COG null cells possess altered content and subcellular localization of ATP7A and CTR1 (SLC31A1), the transporter required for copper uptake, as well as decreased total cellular copper, and impaired copper-dependent metabolic responses.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot and surface biotinylation experiments in Figure 6.

claim: COG null cells possess altered content and subcellular localization of CTR1.
source: COG null cells possess altered content and subcellular localization of ATP7A and CTR1 (SLC31A1), the transporter required for copper uptake, as well as decreased total cellular copper, and impaired copper-dependent metabolic responses.
evidence: This is demonstrated by surface biotinylation experiments in Figure 6.

claim: COG null cells have decreased total cellular copper.
source: COG null cells possess altered content and subcellular localization of ATP7A and CTR1 (SLC31A1), the transporter required for copper uptake, as well as decreased total cellular copper, and impaired copper-dependent metabolic responses.
evidence: This is demonstrated by inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry measurements in Figure 7A.

claim: COG null cells have impaired copper-dependent metabolic responses.
source: COG null cells possess altered content and subcellular localization of ATP7A and CTR1 (SLC31A1), the transporter required for copper uptake, as well as decreased total cellular copper, and impaired copper-dependent metabolic responses.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT assays in Figure 8.

claim: Changes in the expression of ATP7A and COG subunits in Drosophila neurons altered synapse development in larvae.
source: Changes in the expression of ATP7A and COG subunits in Drosophila neurons altered synapse development in larvae and copper-induced mortality of adult flies.
evidence: This is demonstrated by neuromuscular junction analysis in Figure 9.

claim: Changes in the expression of ATP7A and COG subunits in Drosophila neurons altered copper-induced mortality of adult flies.
source: Changes in the expression of ATP7A and COG subunits in Drosophila neurons altered synapse development in larvae and copper-induced mortality of adult flies.
evidence: This is demonstrated by copper feeding experiments in Figure 10.

claim: Copper, iron, and manganese act as micronutrients, yet in excess behave as environmental neurotoxicants.
source: Copper, iron, and manganese act as micronutrients, yet in excess behave as environmental neurotoxicants (Bush, 2013; Perl and Olanow, 2007; Wright and Metals, 2007; Madsen and Gitlin, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Mutations in metal membrane transport and chaperoning mechanisms cause neurodegenerative disorders in both children and adults.
source: Mutations in these metal membrane transport and chaperoning mechanisms cause neurodegenerative disorders in both children and adults (Madsen and Gitlin, 2007; Kaler, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cellular copper content is regulated by two chief transporters, ATP7A and CTR1 (SLC31A1).
source: Cellular copper content is regulated by two chief transporters, ATP7A and CTR1 (SLC31A1) (Madsen and Gitlin, 2007; Kaler, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ATP7A resides at the Golgi apparatus where it sequesters copper topologically into the Golgi lumen and away from the cytoplasm.
source: ATP7A resides at the Golgi apparatus where it sequesters copper topologically into the Golgi lumen and away from the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: CTR1 localizes to the plasma membrane where it transports copper into the cytoplasm from the extracellular milieu.
source: In contrast, CTR1 localizes to the plasma membrane where it transports copper into the cytoplasm from the extracellular milieu (Kaler, 2011; Lutsenko et al., 2007; Polishchuk and Lutsenko, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: After an extracellular copper challenge, ATP7A translocates from the Golgi complex to the plasma membrane where it extrudes copper out of cells.
source: After an extracellular copper challenge, ATP7A translocates from the Golgi complex to the plasma membrane where it extrudes copper out of cells while CTR1 undergoes copper-dependent endocytosis, thus down-regulating CTR1-dependent copper transport across the plasma membrane (Kaler, 2011; Lutsenko et al., 2007; Polishchuk and Lutsenko, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: CTR1 undergoes copper-dependent endocytosis, thus down-regulating CTR1-dependent copper transport across the plasma membrane.
source: After an extracellular copper challenge, ATP7A translocates from the Golgi complex to the plasma membrane where it extrudes copper out of cells while CTR1 undergoes copper-dependent endocytosis, thus down-regulating CTR1-dependent copper transport across the plasma membrane (Kaler, 2011; Lutsenko et al., 2007; Polishchuk and Lutsenko, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ATP7A loss-of-function genetic defects cause three neurological diseases, including Menkes disease (OMIM 309400), occipital horn syndrome (OMIM 304150), and X-linked distal spinal muscular atrophy type 3 (OMIM 300489).
source: ATP7A loss-of-function genetic defects cause three neurological diseases, including Menkes disease (OMIM 309400), occipital horn syndrome (OMIM 304150), and X-linked distal spinal muscular atrophy type 3 (OMIM 300489).
evidence: This is supported by established medical knowledge and OMIM database references.

claim: Menkes causing mutations systemically deplete organisms and cells of copper due to defective gut copper uptake.
source: Menkes causing mutations systemically deplete organisms and cells of copper due to defective gut copper uptake, which in turn reduces the activity of cuproenzymes involved in neurotransmitter, neuropeptide, melanin, mitochondrial respiration, and extracellular matrix synthesis (Kaler, 2011; Lutsenko et al., 2007; Menkes, 1999; Menkes et al., 1962; Kennerson et al., 2010; Tümer, 2013; Kaler et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: In SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells, the addition of increasing amounts of copper leads to an increase of ATP7A at the cell surface.
source: In SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells, the addition of increasing amounts of copper leads to an increase of ATP7A at the cell surface as measured by surface biotinylation followed by streptavidin pull-down (lanes 1'−4'), while the total levels of ATP7A remain unchanged (lanes 1–4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by surface biotinylation experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The total levels of ATP7A remain unchanged with copper addition in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: In SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells, the addition of increasing amounts of copper leads to an increase of ATP7A at the cell surface as measured by surface biotinylation followed by streptavidin pull-down (lanes 1'−4'), while the total levels of ATP7A remain unchanged (lanes 1–4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Transferrin receptor shows consistent surface expression regardless of copper addition.
source: Transferrin receptor shows consistent surface expression regardless of copper addition (lanes 1'−4').
evidence: This is demonstrated by surface biotinylation experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The monoclonal ATP7A antibody recognizes a single band by immunoblot that is missing in ATP7A null human Menkes fibroblasts.
source: The monoclonal ATP7A antibody used in these studies recognizes a single band by immunoblot. This band is missing in ATP7A null human Menkes fibroblasts (lane 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ATP7A and dopamine beta hydroxylase (DBH) co-immunoprecipitate.
source: The presence of ATP7A and one previously described interactor, dopamine beta hydroxylase (DBH), was confirmed by immunoblot of isolated cross-linked complexes (Figure 1D) (Gokhale et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation followed by immunoblot shown in Figure 1D, and supported by a citation.

claim: Protein complexes copurifying with ATP7A isolated from BCS or copper-treated cells were not evidently different.
source: Protein complexes copurifying with ATP7A isolated from BCS or copper-treated cells were not evidently different (Figure 1D, compare lanes 2 and 2' and traces, and Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by silver stain analysis shown in Figure 1D and mass spectrometry data in Figure 2C.

claim: One hundred and thirty four proteins co-isolated with ATP7A regardless of whether cells were incubated with BCS or copper.
source: One hundred and thirty four proteins co-isolated with ATP7A regardless of whether cells were incubated with BCS or copper (Figure 2A and C, see Supplementary files 1–3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The overlap between the 541 ATP7A interactors and the CRAPome was just 31 proteins, a 5.7% overlap.
source: The overlap between our five hundred and forty one ATP7A interactors and the CRAPome was just thirty one proteins, a 5.7% overlap (Figure 2C, CRAPome, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison with the CRAPome database shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The ATP7A interactome includes known ATP7A interactors such as dopamine beta hydroxylase.
source: The interactome includes known ATP7A interactors such as dopamine beta hydroxylase (Gokhale et al., 2015a); subunits of the WASH complex, FAM21 and WASH1 (Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Ryder et al., 2013); subunits of the retromer complex, VPS26 and 35 (Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Steinberg et al., 2013); and components of clathrin-coated vesicles such as CLTB (Holloway et al., 2013; Montpetit et al., 2008; Yi and Kaler, 2015; Hirst et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The ATP7A interactome includes subunits of the WASH complex, FAM21 and WASH1.
source: The interactome includes known ATP7A interactors such as dopamine beta hydroxylase (Gokhale et al., 2015a); subunits of the WASH complex, FAM21 and WASH1 (Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Ryder et al., 2013); subunits of the retromer complex, VPS26 and 35 (Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Steinberg et al., 2013); and components of clathrin-coated vesicles such as CLTB (Holloway et al., 2013; Montpetit et al., 2008; Yi and Kaler, 2015; Hirst et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The ATP7A interactome includes subunits of the retromer complex, VPS26 and 35.
source: The interactome includes known ATP7A interactors such as dopamine beta hydroxylase (Gokhale et al., 2015a); subunits of the WASH complex, FAM21 and WASH1 (Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Ryder et al., 2013); subunits of the retromer complex, VPS26 and 35 (Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Steinberg et al., 2013); and components of clathrin-coated vesicles such as CLTB (Holloway et al., 2013; Montpetit et al., 2008; Yi and Kaler, 2015; Hirst et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The ATP7A interactome includes components of clathrin-coated vesicles such as CLTB.
source: The interactome includes known ATP7A interactors such as dopamine beta hydroxylase (Gokhale et al., 2015a); subunits of the WASH complex, FAM21 and WASH1 (Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Ryder et al., 2013); subunits of the retromer complex, VPS26 and 35 (Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Steinberg et al., 2013); and components of clathrin-coated vesicles such as CLTB (Holloway et al., 2013; Montpetit et al., 2008; Yi and Kaler, 2015; Hirst et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Gene ontological categories were enriched in Golgi-related terms such as Golgi transport complex (GO:0017119, p<5E-6), which contained six of the eight subunits of the Golgi localized COG tethering complex.
source: Gene ontological categories were enriched in Golgi-related terms such as Golgi transport complex (GO:0017119, p<5E-6), which contained six of the eight subunits of the Golgi localized COG tethering complex.
evidence: This is demonstrated by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Bioinformatics identified neuronal ontological terms including growth cone, neuron projection, and dendrite (GO:004300, 0030426, 003042, respectively; all p<10E-4).
source: Additionally, bioinformatics identified neuronal ontological terms including growth cone, neuron projection, and dendrite (GO:004300, 0030426, 003042, respectively; all p<10E-4, Figure 3A, Supplementary file 3A–B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The COG complex was among the most prominently enriched complexes present in the ATP7A interactome.
source: In fact, the COG complex was among the most prominently enriched complexes present in the ATP7A interactome (CORUM database, Figure 3D, combined score >7, see Supplementary file 3B) (Ruepp et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CORUM database analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Gene products contained in the ATP7A interactome were significantly enriched in categories describing mouse phenotypes such as abnormal brain-neuronal morphology and neurodegeneration.
source: Analysis of gene sets describing mouse phenotypes demonstrated that gene products contained in the ATP7A interactome were significantly enriched in categories describing neuronal pathology such as abnormal brain-neuronal morphology and neurodegeneration (Figure 3E, combined score >9.5, Supplementary file 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mouse phenotype database analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The ATP7A interactome enriched 62 neurodegeneration associated or causative genes (MeSH, Medical Subject Heading C10.574, p<0.0001).
source: The ATP7A interactome enriched 62 neurodegeneration associated or causative genes (MeSH, Medical Subject Heading C10.574, p<0.0001), which include COG2, VPS26, VPS35, DBH, and NSF.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GDA bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: 181 gene products contained in the ATP7A interactome were associated with mental disorders (Medical Subject Heading F03, p<0.0001).
source: Moreover, 181 gene products contained in the ATP7A interactome were associated with mental disorders (Medical Subject Heading F03, p<0.0001, Supplementary file 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GDA bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The ATP7A monoclonal antibody co-immunoprecipitated strumpellin and clathrin heavy chain.
source: The ATP7A monoclonal antibody co-immunoprecipitated strumpellin and clathrin heavy chain, and other proteins belonging to the ATP7A interactome listed above (Figure 5A, lane 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation followed by immunoblot shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The addition of ATP7A immunogenic peptide prevented the coprecipitation of ATP7A with selected interactome components.
source: The addition of ATP7A immunogenic peptide prevented the coprecipitation of ATP7A with these selected interactome components (Figure 5A, lane 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Abundant cytosolic proteins including actin, several peroxiredoxins, thioredoxin, and the ubiquitin hydrolase UCHL1 did not co-isolate with ATP7A.
source: These proteins include actin, several peroxiredoxins, thioredoxin, and the ubiquitin hydrolase UCHL1 (Figure 5B). None of these proteins co-isolated with ATP7A even in the presence of a crosslinker (Figure 5B, lane 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation followed by immunoblot shown in Figure 5B.

claim: COG null cell lines exhibited decreased expression of GPP130.
source: Both COG null cell lines exhibited decreased expression of a known COG-dependent and Golgi-localized membrane protein, GPP130 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: GPP130 protein was found to migrate faster during SDS-PAGE in COG null cells, an indication of defective GPP130 glycosylation.
source: In addition, the GPP130 protein was found to migrate faster during SDS-PAGE, an indication of defective GPP130 glycosylation in COG null cells (Figure 6A) (Sohda et al., 2010; Oka et al., 2004; Zolov and Lupashin, 2005).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 6A and supported by citations.

claim: ATP7A expression was reduced by ~25–50% in COG null cells.
source: Similarly, ATP7A expression was reduced by ~25–50% (Figure 6A–B), and ATP7A SDS-PAGE migration was increased in COG-null cell lines (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: ATP7A SDS-PAGE migration was increased in COG-null cell lines.
source: Similarly, ATP7A expression was reduced by ~25–50% (Figure 6A–B), and ATP7A SDS-PAGE migration was increased in COG-null cell lines (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Normalized surface levels of ATP7A were decreased in COG1Δ/Δ HEK293 cells as compared to controls.
source: Normalized surface levels of ATP7A were decreased in COG1Δ/Δ HEK293 cells as compared to controls (Figure 6C, compare lanes 5–6, Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by surface biotinylation experiments shown in Figure 6C and quantified in Figure 6E.

claim: Normalized ATP7A surface levels in COG1Δ/Δ HEK293 cells did not change after copper addition.
source: In contrast, normalized ATP7A surface levels in COG1Δ/Δ HEK293 cells did not change after copper (Figure 6C, compare lanes 5 and 7 and 6 and 8; Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by surface biotinylation experiments shown in Figure 6C and quantified in Figure 6E.

claim: The CTR1 antibody recognized monomeric and oligomeric species when CTR1 was enriched in cell surface biotinylated proteins.
source: The CTR1 antibody recognized monomeric and oligomeric species when CTR1 was enriched in cell surface biotinylated proteins, thus we could not assess CTR1 total cellular expression (Figure 6C compare inputs 1–2 to lanes 5–8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Addition of copper to wild type and COG1Δ/Δ HEK293 cells further exacerbated the depletion of CTR1 at the surface.
source: Addition of copper to wild type and COG1Δ/Δ HEK293 cells further exacerbated the depletion of CTR1 at the surface (Figure 6C compare lanes 5 and 7, lanes 6 and 8, and Figure 6F), demonstrating that wild type and COG1Δ/Δ HEK293 cells are responsive to copper challenge.
evidence: This is demonstrated by surface biotinylation experiments shown in Figure 6C and quantified in Figure 6F.

claim: Copper was readily detectable in wild type HEK293 cells.
source: Copper was readily detectable in wild type HEK293 cells. However, copper content in COG-null HEK293 cells was below detection limit (1 ng/sample, Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry measurements shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Copper content in COG-null HEK293 cells was below detection limit (1 ng/sample).
source: Copper was readily detectable in wild type HEK293 cells. However, copper content in COG-null HEK293 cells was below detection limit (1 ng/sample, Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry measurements shown in Figure 7A.

claim: COG-null cellular copper phenotype was selective since zinc levels remained similar to wild type.
source: COG-null cellular copper phenotype was selective since zinc levels remained similar to wild type (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry measurements shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Addition of the copper-selective chelator BCS brought down copper content in wild type cells.
source: Addition of the copper-selective chelator BCS brought down copper content in wild type cells while addition of copper chloride or the copper ionophore disulfiram increased cellular copper levels in all three genotypes (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry measurements shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Addition of copper chloride or the copper ionophore disulfiram increased cellular copper levels in all three genotypes.
source: Addition of the copper-selective chelator BCS brought down copper content in wild type cells while addition of copper chloride or the copper ionophore disulfiram increased cellular copper levels in all three genotypes (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry measurements shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Copper chloride uptake was impaired in COG null cells as compared to wild type HEK293 cells even when COG-null cells were exposed to 25 μM copper.
source: However, copper chloride uptake was impaired in COG null cells as compared to wild type HEK293 cells even when COG-null cells were exposed to 25 μM copper (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry measurements shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Only the addition of the copper ionophore disulfiram increased the copper content at or above wild type levels in COG null HEK293 cells.
source: Only the addition of the copper ionophore disulfiram increased the copper content at or above wild type levels in COG null HEK293 cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry measurements shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Both COG1Δ/Δ and COG8Δ/Δ deficiency doubled ATP7A transcript levels as compared with wild type cells.
source: In stark contrast with the ATP7A protein expression levels, both COG1Δ/Δ and COG8Δ/Δ deficiency doubled ATP7A transcript levels as compared with wild type cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Transcripts encoding metallothioneins IA and IIB were increased only in COG8Δ/Δ.
source: Transcripts encoding metallothioneins IA and IIB were increased only in COG8Δ/Δ (MT1A and MT2A, Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: mRNA levels of two metallochaperones that traffic copper to mitochondria, CCS and COX17, were significantly down-regulated in both COG1Δ/Δ and COG8Δ/Δ cells.
source: However, mRNA levels of two metallochaperones that traffic copper to mitochondria, CCS and COX17, were significantly down-regulated in both COG1Δ/Δ and COG8Δ/Δ cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: CCS mRNA was reduced to 58% in both COG deficient cells.
source: CCS mRNA was reduced to 58% in both COG deficient cells whereas COX17 mRNA was decreased to 64% of the control values.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: COX17 mRNA was decreased to 64% of the control values in COG deficient cells.
source: CCS mRNA was reduced to 58% in both COG deficient cells whereas COX17 mRNA was decreased to 64% of the control values.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: PET191/COA5 mRNA was significantly decreased to ~70% in both COG1Δ/Δ and COG8Δ/Δ HEK293 cells.
source: Of these factors PET191/COA5 mRNA was significantly decreased to ~70% in both COG1Δ/Δ and COG8Δ/Δ HEK293 cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: SCO1 and COX23 were selectively down-regulated in COG1Δ/Δ and COG8Δ/Δ cells, respectively.
source: In contrast, SCO1 and COX23 were selectively down-regulated in COG1Δ/Δ and COG8Δ/Δ cells, respectively (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Wild type cells exposed to low copper, 3–20 µM, increased MTT reduction as compared to wild type cells incubated with media alone.
source: Wild type cells exposed to low copper, 3–20 µM, increased MTT reduction as compared to wild type cells incubated with media alone (Figure 8A, grey symbols).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT assay shown in Figure 8A.

claim: COG1Δ/Δ, COG8Δ/Δ, and COG1,8Δ/Δ HEK293 cells exposed to low copper failed to increase MTT metabolization.
source: In contrast, COG1Δ/Δ, COG8Δ/Δ, and COG1,8Δ/Δ HEK293 cells exposed to low copper failed to increase MTT metabolization (Figure 8A, blue symbols and Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT assay shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Irrespective of the cell genotype, all cells experienced a decrease of MTT metabolization at copper concentrations above 50 µM, likely due to copper toxicity.
source: Irrespective of the cell genotype, all cells experienced a decrease of MTT metabolization at copper concentrations above 50 µM, likely due to copper toxicity (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT assay shown in Figure 8A, with speculation about the cause.

claim: COG- and copper-dependent phenotypes do not reflect general cellular sensitivity to metal-based toxicants as assessed with cisplatin.
source: These COG- and copper-dependent phenotypes do not reflect general cellular sensitivity to metal-based toxicants as assessed with cisplatin, a cytotoxic agent whose import into HEK293 cells does not require CTR1 copper transporter activity (Figure 8B) (Bompiani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT assay with cisplatin shown in Figure 8B and supported by a citation.

claim: Addition of increasing disulfiram to wild type and COG-null HEK293 cells did not affect MTT activity at low concentrations, yet disulfiram above 25 nM decreased MTT activity.
source: Addition of increasing disulfiram to wild type and COG-null HEK293 cells did not affect MTT activity at low concentrations, yet disulfiram above 25 nM decreased MTT activity (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT assay shown in Figure 8C.

claim: None of the disulfiram concentrations significantly affected cell numbers.
source: None of these disulfiram concentrations significantly affected cell numbers (Figure 8E) indicating that MTT metabolization was impaired by the copper chelation activity of disulfiram at high doses.
evidence: This is demonstrated by crystal violet staining shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Loading cells with copper using low concentrations of disulfiram (<25 nM) significantly increased MTT metabolization in COG1Δ/Δ and COG8Δ/Δ HEK293 cells as compared to wild type controls.
source: Loading cells with copper using low concentrations of disulfiram (<25 nM) significantly increased MTT metabolization in COG1Δ/Δ and COG8Δ/Δ HEK293 cells as compared to wild type controls (Figure 8D, compare gray and blue symbols).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT assay shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Overexpression of ATP7A reduced the cumulative synapse branch length in Drosophila neuromuscular junction.
source: Overexpression of ATP7A reduced the cumulative synapse branch length; thus, inducing a collapse of the synapse as measured as an increased synaptic bouton density (Figure 9A image C155>UAS-ATP7A, Figure 9B–C, column 4. Compare 4 to control columns 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by neuromuscular junction analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: Overexpression of ATP7A induced a collapse of the synapse as measured as an increased synaptic bouton density.
source: Overexpression of ATP7A reduced the cumulative synapse branch length; thus, inducing a collapse of the synapse as measured as an increased synaptic bouton density (Figure 9A image C155>UAS-ATP7A, Figure 9B–C, column 4. Compare 4 to control columns 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by neuromuscular junction analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: Animals carrying one copy of the null allele cog1e02840 increase cumulative synapse branch length while maintaining wild type synaptic bouton density.
source: In contrast, animals carrying one copy of the null allele cog1e02840 increase cumulative synapse branch length while maintaining wild type synaptic bouton density (Figure 9A–C, column 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by neuromuscular junction analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: Overexpression of ATP7A in cog1e02840 flies restored synaptic bouton density to wild type levels.
source: As predicted by our hypothesis, overexpression of ATP7A in cog1e02840 flies restored synaptic bouton density to wild type levels (Figure 9A and B, compare columns 4 and 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by neuromuscular junction analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: Copper feeding progressively increased mortality in wild type male and female adults over a period of three days.
source: Copper feeding progressively increased mortality in wild type male (Figure 10A) and female adults (Figure 10B) over a period of three days.
evidence: This is demonstrated by copper feeding experiments shown in Figure 10A-B.

claim: Overexpression of ATP7A in adult dopaminergic neurons was sufficient to significantly protect males and female adult animals from the toxic effect of copper feed at 48 hr.
source: Overexpression of ATP7A in adult dopaminergic neurons was sufficient to significantly protect males and female adult animals from the toxic effect of copper feed at 48 hr (Figure 10A–B, (Ddc>UAS-ATP7A)).
evidence: This is demonstrated by copper feeding experiments shown in Figure 10A-B.

claim: Mutation of the COG complex subunit cog1 protected animals from copper diet induced death.
source: Similarly, mutation of the COG complex subunit cog1 protected animals from copper diet induced death (Figure 10A–B, (Ddc x cog1e02840)).
evidence: This is demonstrated by copper feeding experiments shown in Figure 10A-B.

claim: The mortality phenotype observed in animals overexpressing ATP7A was restored to the levels of wild type lethality by adding in trans a genetic defect in cog1.
source: In contrast, the mortality phenotype observed in animals overexpressing ATP7A was restored to the levels of wild type lethality by adding in trans a genetic defect in cog1 (Figure 10A–B, (UAS-ATP7A; Ddc x cog1e02840)).
evidence: This is demonstrated by copper feeding experiments shown in Figure 10A-B.

claim: Mortality was negligible when copper was omitted from the diet fed to animals of any genotype.
source: Importantly, mortality was negligible when copper was omitted from the diet fed to animals of any genotype (Figure 10C–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by control feeding experiments shown in Figure 10C-D.

claim: COG is a Golgi vesicle tether necessary for intra Golgi vesicular traffic and the retention of Golgi-localized enzymes at the Golgi complex, such as glycosyltransferases.
source: COG is a Golgi vesicle tether necessary for intra Golgi vesicular traffic and the retention of Golgi-localized enzymes at the Golgi complex, such as glycosyltransferases (Climer et al., 2015; Willett et al., 2013; Miller and Ungar, 2012; Ungar et al., 2002; Kranz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: COG genetic defects cause disruption of the Golgi complex function characterized by the loss of Golgi-resident enzymes and alterations in the glycosylation of membrane proteins traversing the exocytic route.
source: COG genetic defects cause disruption of the Golgi complex function characterized by the loss of Golgi-resident enzymes and alterations in the glycosylation of membrane proteins traversing the exocytic route.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: COG mutations cause a systemic disorder that includes cerebral atrophy, developmental delay, hypotonia, ataxia and epilepsy.
source: These COG mutations cause a systemic disorder that includes cerebral atrophy, developmental delay, hypotonia, ataxia and epilepsy (Climer et al., 2015; Willett et al., 2013; Miller and Ungar, 2012; Ungar et al., 2002; Kranz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The ATP7A interactome encompasses a novel COG-dependent mechanism to specify neuronal development and survival.
source: We conclude that the ATP7A interactome encompasses a novel COG-dependent mechanism to specify neuronal development and survival.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The COG complex is a hub where two copper transporters, ATP7A and CTR1, converge to regulate cellular copper content, homeostasis, synapse development and copper-induced neurodegeneration.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the COG complex is a hub where two copper transporters, ATP7A and CTR1, converge to regulate cellular copper content, homeostasis, synapse development and copper-induced neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Disulfiram is a cell permeant copper chelation agent that inhibits copper dependent enzymes in diverse compartments including mitochondria.
source: Disulfiram is a cell permeant copper chelation agent that inhibits copper dependent enzymes in diverse compartments including mitochondria (Simonian et al., 1992; Kuroda and Cuéllar, 1993; Goldstein, 1966; Gaval-Cruz and Weinshenker, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Disulfiram complexed with copper increases metal cellular levels.
source: However, disulfiram complexed with copper increases metal cellular levels (Cen et al., 2004; Allensworth et al., 2015) (Figure 7A), and rescues respiration phenotypes in CTR1 null cells (Schlecht et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and demonstrated in Figure 7A.

claim: Disulfiram rescues respiration phenotypes in CTR1 null cells.
source: However, disulfiram complexed with copper increases metal cellular levels (Cen et al., 2004; Allensworth et al., 2015) (Figure 7A), and rescues respiration phenotypes in CTR1 null cells (Schlecht et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: RNAi or mutation of COG subunits alters copper content in mammalian cells and yeast, respectively.
source: Our hypothesis that copper homeostasis is impaired in COGΔ/Δ cells is supported by reports describing that RNAi or mutation of COG subunits alters copper content in mammalian cells and yeast, respectively (Schlecht et al., 2014; Malinouski et al., 2014) and by our data that levels of copper and copper sensitive transcripts encoding proteins present in or transferring copper to different subcellular compartments are altered in COG null cells (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Copper regulatory genes are known to undergo coordinated regulation in response to changing copper levels.
source: Copper regulatory genes are known to undergo coordinated regulation in response to changing copper levels, and we found that multiple copper sensitive transcripts are decreased in COGΔ/Δ cells (Barresi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The expression of CTR1 is modulated by the mitochondrial metallochaperone SCO1.
source: Genetic evidence indicates that the expression of CTR1 is modulated by the mitochondrial metallochaperone SCO1 (Hlynialuk et al., 2015), down-regulation of mitochondrial components including complex I subunits (NDUFB4, NDUFA1) and the mitochondrial transporter SLC25A41 lead to global cellular changes in copper (Malinouski et al., 2014), and the elimination of ATP7A rescues mitochondrial metallochaperone mutant phenotypes (Malinouski et al., 2014; Leary et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Down-regulation of mitochondrial components including complex I subunits (NDUFB4, NDUFA1) and the mitochondrial transporter SLC25A41 lead to global cellular changes in copper.
source: Genetic evidence indicates that the expression of CTR1 is modulated by the mitochondrial metallochaperone SCO1 (Hlynialuk et al., 2015), down-regulation of mitochondrial components including complex I subunits (NDUFB4, NDUFA1) and the mitochondrial transporter SLC25A41 lead to global cellular changes in copper (Malinouski et al., 2014), and the elimination of ATP7A rescues mitochondrial metallochaperone mutant phenotypes (Malinouski et al., 2014; Leary et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The elimination of ATP7A rescues mitochondrial metallochaperone mutant phenotypes.
source: Genetic evidence indicates that the expression of CTR1 is modulated by the mitochondrial metallochaperone SCO1 (Hlynialuk et al., 2015), down-regulation of mitochondrial components including complex I subunits (NDUFB4, NDUFA1) and the mitochondrial transporter SLC25A41 lead to global cellular changes in copper (Malinouski et al., 2014), and the elimination of ATP7A rescues mitochondrial metallochaperone mutant phenotypes (Malinouski et al., 2014; Leary et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Disruptions in copper homeostasis have been implicated in several other prevalent neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease.
source: Along with the neurodegeneration characteristic of Menkes disease, disruptions in copper homeostasis have been implicated in several other prevalent neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease (Greenough et al., 2016; Davies et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Therapeutic modulation of copper levels may be effective in alleviating symptoms of or delaying the onset of Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease.
source: There is evidence that therapeutic modulation of copper levels may be effective in alleviating symptoms of or delaying the onset of Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease, yet there are gaps in our understanding of the regulation of copper homeostasis, particularly in the brain (Sparks and Schreurs, 2003; Brewer, 2015; Rose et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Polymorphisms in genes encoding the COG complex subunits COG4, 6, and 8 associate with neurodegenerative and neurobehavioral phenotypes in humans.
source: Polymorphisms in genes encoding the COG complex subunits COG4, 6, and 8 associate with neurodegenerative and neurobehavioral phenotypes in humans (Li et al., 2008; Scharf et al., 2013; Kendler et al., 2011; Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: COG2 subunit is one of 42 gene products present in the ATP7A interactome associated with tauopathies and Alzheimer's disease.
source: Our bioinformatic studies also indicate that the COG2 subunit is one of 42 gene products present in the ATP7A interactome associated with tauopathies and Alzheimer's disease; one of fourteen genes products associated with Parkinson's disease; and one of the 49 gene products in the ATP7A interactome associated with neurocognitive disorders, such as dementia (Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: COG2 subunit is one of fourteen gene products associated with Parkinson's disease in the ATP7A interactome.
source: Our bioinformatic studies also indicate that the COG2 subunit is one of 42 gene products present in the ATP7A interactome associated with tauopathies and Alzheimer's disease; one of fourteen genes products associated with Parkinson's disease; and one of the 49 gene products in the ATP7A interactome associated with neurocognitive disorders, such as dementia (Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: COG2 subunit is one of the 49 gene products in the ATP7A interactome associated with neurocognitive disorders, such as dementia.
source: Our bioinformatic studies also indicate that the COG2 subunit is one of 42 gene products present in the ATP7A interactome associated with tauopathies and Alzheimer's disease; one of fourteen genes products associated with Parkinson's disease; and one of the 49 gene products in the ATP7A interactome associated with neurocognitive disorders, such as dementia (Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Deletions of COG complex subunits lead to type II congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG II) and are strongly associated with cerebral atrophy, developmental delay, hypotonia, ataxia and epilepsy.
source: Deletions of COG complex subunits lead to type II congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG II) and are strongly associated with cerebral atrophy, developmental delay, hypotonia, ataxia and epilepsy (Foulquier et al., 2006; Kodera et al., 2015; Reynders et al., 2009; Paesold-Burda et al., 2009; Fung et al., 2012; Rymen et al., 2012; Lübbehusen et al., 2010; Huybrechts et al., 2012; Shaheen et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2004; Morava et al., 2007; Zeevaert et al., 2009; Foulquier et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: COG mutations drastically decreased the cellular copper levels.
source: Since COG mutations drastically decreased the cellular copper levels (Figure 7A), it is possible that COG neurological phenotypes reflect in part decreased neuronal copper much like is the case in Menkes disease.
evidence: This is demonstrated by inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry measurements shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Mutations in cog1 prevent toxicity of dietary copper in Drosophila.
source: Mutations in cog1 prevent toxicity of dietary copper in Drosophila (Figure 10) supporting this concept of decrease copper content in COG deficient neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by copper feeding experiments shown in Figure 10.

claim: Common phenotypes between Menkes and congenital disorders of glycosylation include developmental delay, seizures, hypotonia and cerebral atrophy.
source: Common phenotypes include developmental delay, seizures, hypotonia and cerebral atrophy (Kaler, 2011; Menkes, 1999; Menkes et al., 1962; Kennerson et al., 2010; Tümer, 2013; Kaler et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Part of the neurological phenotypes in COG genetic defects may be due to impaired copper content and metabolism.
source: Our findings suggest that part of the neurological phenotypes in COG genetic defects may be due to impaired copper content and metabolism as we report here.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Essential mineral homeostasis, such as copper, results from coordinated multicompartment metabolite sensing and response mechanisms.
source: Our finding that the COG complex, a Golgi localized tether is implicated in mitochondrial copper homeostasis indicates that essential mineral homeostasis, such as copper, results from coordinated multicompartment metabolite sensing and response mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ATP7A possesses 664 predicted and 13 experimentally tested interactors according to a comprehensive computational interactome of the human genome.
source: ATP7A possesses 664 predicted and 13 experimentally tested interactors according to a comprehensive computational interactome of the human genome (Garzón et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The experimentally generated ATP7A interactome includes 541 proteins, of which only 21 proteins are in common with a computational ATP7A interactome.
source: Our experimentally generated ATP7A interactome includes 541 proteins, of which only 21 proteins are in common with a computational ATP7A interactome.
evidence: This is a comparison of the experimental data with published computational predictions.

claim: The majority of the ATP7A interactome components identified here consisted of uncharacterized relationships.
source: Therefore, the majority of the ATP7A interactome components identified here consisted of uncharacterized relationships.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison with computational predictions.

claim: DSP is a short arm 12 Å cross-linker, which is cell permeant and cleavable by reducing agents.
source: DSP is a short arm 12 Å cross-linker, which is cell permeant and cleavable by reducing agents (Alloza et al., 2004; Lomant and Fairbanks, 1976; Zlatic et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cross-linking increases the coverage of interactome components co-purifying with membrane proteins of complex topology, such as ATP7A.
source: Cross-linking increases the coverage of interactome components co-purifying with membrane proteins of complex topology, such as ATP7A (Gokhale et al., 2012; Perez-Cornejo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Three COG subunits were present in both BCS and copper-treated samples (COG2, 4 and 7).
source: Three of these six COG subunits were identified in the BSC and copper-challenged ATP7A interactomes (Figure 2C, COG2, 4 and 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cytochrome c oxidase requires copper as a cofactor.
source: Cytochrome c oxidase, though not directly downstream of ATP7A, requires copper as a cofactor, and thus mitochondrial function is impaired by decreased activity of cytochrome c oxidase when copper delivery to mitochondria is impaired (Leary et al., 2004, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mitochondrial function is impaired by decreased activity of cytochrome c oxidase when copper delivery to mitochondria is impaired.
source: Cytochrome c oxidase, though not directly downstream of ATP7A, requires copper as a cofactor, and thus mitochondrial function is impaired by decreased activity of cytochrome c oxidase when copper delivery to mitochondria is impaired (Leary et al., 2004, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ATP7A overexpression cell-autonomously decreases cellular levels of copper due to ATP7A mistargeting to the cell surface.
source: We focused on ATP7A overexpression because it cell-autonomously decreases cellular levels of copper due to ATP7A mistargeting to the cell surface (Hwang et al., 2014; Lye et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tetrazolium is reduced into formazan by NAD(P)H-dependent oxidoreductases and dehydrogenases localized to cytoplasm and mitochondria.
source: Tetrazolium is reduced into formazan by NAD(P)H-dependent oxidoreductases and dehydrogenases localized to cytoplasm and mitochondria (Berridge et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Cisplatin is a cytotoxic agent whose import into HEK293 cells does not require CTR1 copper transporter activity.
source: These COG- and copper-dependent phenotypes do not reflect general cellular sensitivity to metal-based toxicants as assessed with cisplatin, a cytotoxic agent whose import into HEK293 cells does not require CTR1 copper transporter activity (Figure 8B) (Bompiani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.
